raw_case_text:
A 6-month-old boy with hydrocephalus was referred to our hospital in 2008. The hydrocephalus during the first admission was confirmed by computed tomography (CT) scan. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) did not reveal any abnormality.
A VP shunt was inserted in June 2008 and the infant was discharged in acceptable condition, with good control of hydrocephalus confirmed by another CT scan on discharge day. Approximately 16 months after insertion of the VP shunt, the child was readmitted with a one-week history of fever (up to 38.5 C), and acute abdominal pain. The diagnosis was brucellosis based on serum agglutination test 1/640 and 1/1280 three days later. A titre of 1/320 measured in 2 mercaptoethanol (2ME) test. The patient was treated with trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, rifampin, and gentamicin. His blood culture was negative.
The Ascitic fluid examination showed a glucose level of 89 mg/dL, a protein level of 5800 mg/dL, white blood cell (WBC) count was 480 (10% polymorphonuclear cells and 90% mononuclear), and the red blood cell (RBC) count was 4800.
After 4 months, he was again admitted to our hospital with drowsiness, vomiting and fever. Clinical diagnosis was suggestive for a VP shunt infection. Laboratory results were as follows: Hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL; WBC count, 6.1x103 cells/mm3. 
A sample of ventricular CSF analyzed was slightly xanthochromic and contained a total of 4000 cells (70% polymorphonuclear cells and 30% lymphocytes), 80 mg/ dL glucose, and 192 mg/dL protein. No organisms were observed on the direct gram-stained smear. 
Blood culture was sterile and CSF serological test was positive (Brucella agglutinin titer was 1/80).
The patient responded well to a course of rifampin, gentamicin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily. Three days later the shunt was extracted. He was well on three follow-up visits at the outpatient clinic and the latest follow-up visit was 12 months after the diagnosis has been made. Figure 1 and 2 show Brain CT scan before and after extracting the VP shunt, respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-month-old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt presented with drowsiness, vomiting, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed with hydrocephalus at 6 months of age and received a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt in June 2008. Approximately 16 months later (at 22 months of age), he was readmitted with a 1-week history of fever (up to 38.5 °C) and acute abdominal pain, receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampin, and gentamicin. Four months later (at 26 months of age), he presented with drowsiness, vomiting, and fever suggestive of VP shunt infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Infantile hydrocephalus treated with ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement in June 2008. Episode of febrile peritonitis/ascites 4 months prior. Animal contact or dairy exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Drowsiness, vomiting, fever; previous acute abdominal pain. Home medications: prior antibiotics (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampin, gentamicin). Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature up to 38.5 °C; drowsiness/lethargy. Abdomen: acute abdominal pain noted during prior admission. Other physical exam details not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Ascitic fluid analysis (prior admission): glucose 89 mg/dL, protein 5,800 mg/dL, WBC count 480/mm^3 (10% polymorphonuclear, 90% mononuclear), RBC count 4,800/mm^3. Readmission blood labs: Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, WBC count 6.1 x 10^3 cells/mm^3. Blood cultures: sterile during both admissions.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT scan: hydrocephalus on initial presentation, with adequate control on post-shunt imaging; pre- and post-extraction CT scans confirmed ventricular configuration. Ventricular CSF analysis: slightly xanthochromic, total cell count 4,000 cells/mm^3 (70% polymorphonuclear cells, 30% lymphocytes), glucose 80 mg/dL, protein 192 mg/dL; Gram-stained smear: no organisms observed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt infection and neurobrucellosis / brucellar peritonitis.
Confirmation: Initial admission serum agglutination test was 1/640, rising to 1/1280 three days later, with 2-mercaptoethanol (2ME) titer of 1/320. Readmission ventricular CSF serology was positive with a Brucella agglutinin titer of 1/80. Blood cultures were sterile.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous/oral rifampin, gentamicin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily, with complete surgical extraction of the infected VP shunt 3 days into therapy. Patient responded well and remained clinically healthy across outpatient follow-ups up to 12 months post-diagnosis.
